description: A team of 5 with 4 gals and one guy tackling the issue of circadian rhythm changes within astronauts in space. Looking to personalize it to individual astronauts to optimize their circadian rhythms and sleep within their space missions.
summary: ORBITAL is a personalized circadian health monitor that learns each astronaut's individual body clock from wearable light and sleep data, then predicts circadian drift before it happens and recommends lighting adjustments to prevent it. Astronauts on the ISS experience 16 sunrises every 24 hours, which breaks the natural light cues their circadian systems depend on. That leads 71–78% to rely on sleep medication and shortens average in-flight sleep to 6 hours. ORBITAL's flight surgeon dashboard shows each crewmember's modeled melatonin onset, their deviation from the mission sleep window, and a personalized lighting plan using the ISS's three real light modes that shifts their body clock back on target within 14 nights. By treating circadian alignment as an individual biology problem rather than a scheduling problem, ORBITAL targets a reduction in preventable medication nights from 71–78% toward the 11% rate observed in circadian-aligned sleep episodes.
details:
What it does: ORBITAL is a web-based flight surgeon dashboard with two panels (Mission Console and Research Data). The Mission Console shows each astronaut's personal circadian profile: their natural day length, how far their melatonin onset has drifted from the mission sleep window, a 6-month forecast of that drift with and without the recommended lighting plan, and a night-by-night lighting prescription using the ISS Solid State Light Assembly's three modes (General 4500K, Pre-sleep 2700K, Alertness 6500K). The Research Data panel lets the team and judges explore the actual NASA data driving the simulation.

How it works: The system uses the Forger99 mathematical model (implemented via the Arcascope circadian open-source library) to simulate each astronaut's circadian phase from their wrist-recorded light and sleep history. It estimates each person's natural day length and phase offset from the last 21 days of data, removes outlier nights (such as docking events), and runs a 90-day forward forecast under two scenarios: current lighting schedule unchanged, or the optimized lighting plan. The lighting plan adjusts pre-sleep light timing, brightness, and morning alertness light to advance melatonin onset toward the goal of 2 hours before the mission bedtime. All adjustments stay within the hardware constraints of the ISS SSLA.

What benefits it has: The system gives flight surgeons an anticipatory tool rather than a reactive one. Lighting adjustments can be pushed 4–6 hours before a predicted bad night. For astronauts, it means fewer sedated nights and more restorative sleep. For missions, it means a crew that can fully rouse in under 60 seconds when a pressure breach or collision warning fires. The projected plan effect shown in the prototype is 1 hour 30 minutes earlier melatonin onset after 14 nights of the prescribed lighting schedule.

What we hope to achieve: A proof of concept that personalized circadian modeling is feasible with existing ISS hardware and NASA datasets. No new sensors. No new drugs. Just smarter use of the light tools already installed.

Tools and languages used: JavaScript (React, frontend), Forger99 circadian model via the Arcascope circadian library (Python/JS), NASA Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) datasets accessed via the OSDR portal, synthetic mission data modeled in the shape of real Actiwatch recordings, NASA DSO 484 prelaunch light-and-sleep shifting study data (accessed via LSDA), UTMB actigraphy ground-based bed-rest study (C1G0001, accessed via LSDA). Claude (Anthropic) was used throughout development for coding assistance, data pipeline design, and GitHub repo construction.
